parsed.explanation: The combined regime stacks an active entry-document exposure (national order barring self-selected markers, February 2025 cable directing refusal where documents cast doubt on sex, with fraud/lifetime-ineligibility consideration; eight governments issued travel advisories) onto nationwide exclusion from government-funded single-sex facilities. The division adds no gender-identity non-discrimination law, surgical-only document changes, a upheld minors' care ban, and House Bill 2009 (2 July 2026) ending hormones/surgery in state prisons with no taper — federal custody separately mandates conversion-therapy-style practice. Official threat-framing and majority public support for restrictive laws are documented. Countervailing: hate-crime statutes covering gender identity, courts enjoining several orders, sanctuary cities, no presentation offence, and no dated trans violence incident here.

entry_documents.exposure: February 2025 executive order and cable bar self-selected gender on passports/visas, stop X markers, and direct refusal where documents cast doubt on sex, with fraud/lifetime-ineligibility consideration; travellers report blocked/confiscated passports and being stranded; eight foreign governments issued advisories.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports remain valid to expiry; litigation by a civil-liberties union is pending; the four-element fraud finding is never automatic and limited waivers exist.
entry_documents.interaction: A document discrepancy at visa adjudication or border inspection escalates into refusal, additional-evidence demands or a fraud inquiry, which can carry the traveller into detention where birth-sex placement and custody care bans then apply.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: House Bill 2009 (effective 2 July 2026) bars state funds for cross-sex hormones or transition surgery in prisons with no taper; the SAFE Act restricts prison treatment. Nationally, the corrections bureau adopted conversion-therapy-style policy (short hair, hormone removal, psychiatric drugs) and stopped reporting trans prisoner counts; immigration custody reports forced labour, beatings, solitary and sexual abuse of trans men.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: State and national hate-crime statutes cover gender identity. No dated custodial violence incident involving a visitor in this division is documented; the cited restroom arrest occurred elsewhere.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Document discrepancy or a minor incident at entry can move a visitor from inspection into custody, where the state care bar, federal inmate policy and birth-sex placement operate together with no documented remedy.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National executive order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities nationwide, applying to visitors with no exemption. The equality map's facility-ban categories are given, but this division's category is not stated; four states criminalise certain facility use (one via trespass requiring refusal to leave after warning).
federal_state_facilities.protection: Facility bans apply chiefly to government-owned settings; 29 states plus units and the capital district have none in mapped categories. Whether this division has a ban or private-setting extension is not documented.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Federal facility exclusion operates regardless of the division's position, and any division-level trespass exposure would compound it for a visitor using public buildings.

care_services.exposure: SAFE Act bars Medicaid payment for gender-affirming care at any age and bans minors' care (upheld January 2026), with a tipline for reporting violations; a November 2026 ballot initiative seeks permanence. National October 2025 proposal would bar public-insurance reimbursement for under-18s. Emergency care for visitors is not documented as restricted.
care_services.protection: Not documented. The dossier does not show emergency or private-care denial to adult trans visitors in this division.
care_services.interaction: Care rules mainly touch residents, but an injured or medicated visitor entering a state facility or custody could encounter the custody funding bar and public-coverage exclusions.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National official hostility: January 2025 orders calling minors' care 'mutilation', directing law enforcement to investigate schools and prosecutors to charge teachers facilitating social transition; May 2026 counterterrorism strategy targets groups 'radically pro-transgender'; December 2025 reward memo uses 'radical gender ideology' in describing violent extremist outlooks. A 2025 poll found 66% backing ASAB on documents and 69% backing the sports ban.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: The reward memo never uses the phrase as a reward criterion and states counterterrorism powers will not target those who merely disagree; several orders are enjoined; advocacy groups litigate openly.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Official framing raises both the probability of scrutiny at document checks and the severity of any ensuing confrontation, while functioning courts partially cushion — but do not remove — that framing.

minors_guardians.exposure: SAFE Act bans under-18 hormones/blockers and all transition surgery, upheld by the state's highest court; the national order directs criminal investigation and prosecution of those facilitating a trans minor's social transition, with funding revocation for schools. The division has no gender-identity non-discrimination law.
minors_guardians.protection: Not documented. The SAFE Act allows those already in treatment to continue, but that is resident care, not visitor protection; no guardian-specific safeguard appears.
minors_guardians.interaction: An adult travelling with a trans minor risks care refusal, hostile official framing of the parent as facilitating transition, and school-adjacent scrutiny; state and national rules reinforce each other rather than offset.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No dated incident of violence against a trans person in this division appears in the sources — silence in an otherwise well-documented dossier, but not proof of safety. National bias statistics show sustained reported hate incidents; majority public support for restrictive laws signals conservative street attitudes. No police targeting of trans people here is documented.
street_violence_police_response.protection: The division's hate-crime statutes explicitly cover gender identity, alongside the national hate-crime statute; ordinary courts function; two cities are trans-sanctuary jurisdictions.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Working hate-crime recourse mitigates private violence, but only within a division lacking any non-discrimination law, so service refusals and harassment have no parallel remedy.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Unresolved: passport litigation pending; several national orders enjoined but operative in patches; SAFE Act sunset (2027) and ballot initiative pending; the driver's-licence policy reversal has no documented challenge; this division's facility-ban category and custody trans-population figures are unreported.
remedies_unknowns.protection: A legal-aid FAQ tracks document rules; a civil-liberties suit challenges the passport policy; courts have blocked multiple orders; sanctuary ordinances operate in two cities; a national risk assessment and travel guides flag conditions.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: The churn between enjoined and effective measures means exposure varies by travel date, but every operative layer — entry documents, federal facilities, custody care — runs in the restrictive direction.

anchor_checks.comparison: Like 0.35-A, a birth-sex facility exclusion applies to visitors (federal buildings nationwide) and politicians and courts largely confirm rather than remedy the wider exclusion regime. This dossier adds entry-stage document exposure with fraud-ineligibility risk and worse custody care denial. It lacks 0.35-A's documented pattern of complaints being rejected in this division, and has no presentation offence or police sweeps — so roughly level, marginally better on enforcement of street-level hostility.

0.45-D pairs repeated invasive transport searches (universal exposure, no remedy) with an otherwise accepting society and no official threat-framing. Here the analogous universal exposure is document/entry scrutiny plus federal facility exclusion, but state hostility is far heavier — executive orders, counterterrorism language, majority public support for restrictions — and custody care is affirmatively cut off. No repeated visitor-facing search or service-refusal survey is documented, yet the net sits below 0.45.

0.65-C rests on documented social acceptance, documents accepted as issued, a dead-letter sexuality statute and ordinary courts awarding relief. This dossier reverses each: entry documents actively restrictive and litigated, official hostility documented, majority social disapproval, custody care bans with no taper. Its genuine positives — hate-crime coverage, partly functioning courts, no presentation offence — are real but much weaker than 0.65-C's acceptance record. Far below.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller meets one system: an entry stage where document discrepancies trigger refusal and possible fraud findings (with eight governments now advising against trans travel), federal buildings where a nationwide birth-sex facility bar applies with no visitor exemption, and a division that adds surgical-only document rules, no gender-identity non-discrimination law, an upheld care ban and — decisive for anyone detained — House Bill 2009 cutting hormones and surgery in state prisons without taper, alongside federal inmate conversion-therapy practice. Social attitudes are majority-restrictive, yet no presentation offence, no documented police targeting or dated violence here, hate-crime coverage and courts that have enjoined several orders provide real but partial mitigation. Exposures are institutional and follow the traveller; protections are contingent and uneven.
